      <content name="altTitle">UTI</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The <span class="qt0">urinary</span> system is the body's drainage system for removing wastes and extra water. It includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder, and a urethra. <span class="qt0">Urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span> (UTIs) are the second most common type of <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> in the body.</p><p>You may have a UTI if you notice:</p><ul><li>Pain or burning when you urinate</li><li>Fever, tiredness, or shakiness</li><li>An urge to urinate often</li><li>Pressure in your lower belly </li><li><span class="qt0">Urine</span> that smells bad or looks cloudy or reddish</li><li>Pain in your back or side below the ribs</li></ul><p>People of any age or sex can get UTIs. But about four times as many women get UTIs as men. You're also at higher risk if you have diabetes, need a tube to drain your bladder, or have a spinal cord injury.</p><p>If you think you have a UTI it is important to see your doctor. Your doctor can tell if you have a UTI with a <span class="qt0">urine</span> test.  Treatment is with antibiotics. </p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/antibiotics.html">
      <content name="title">Antibiotics</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are antibiotics?<p>Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span> in people and animals. They work by killing the bacteria or by making it hard for the bacteria to grow and multiply.</p><p>Antibiotics can be taken in different ways:</p><ul><li>Orally (by mouth). This could be pills, capsules, or liquids.</li><li>Topically. This might be a cream, spray, or ointment that you put on your skin. It could also be eye ointment, eye drops, or ear drops.</li><li>Through an injection or intravenously (IV). This is usually for more serious <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>.</li></ul>What do antibiotics treat?<p>Antibiotics only treat certain bacterial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>, such as strep throat, <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>, and E. coli.</p><p>You may not need to take antibiotics for some bacterial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>. For example, you might not need them for many sinus <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span> or some ear <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>. Taking antibiotics when they're not needed won't help you, and they can have side effects. Your health care provider can decide the best treatment for you when you're sick. Don't ask your provider to prescribe an antibiotic for you.</p>Do antibiotics treat viral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>?<p>Antibiotics do not work on viral <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>. For example, you shouldn't take antibiotics for:</p><ul><li>Colds and runny noses, even if the mucus is thick, yellow, or green</li><li>Most sore throats (except strep throat)</li><li>Flu</li><li>Most cases of bronchitis</li></ul>What are the side effects of antibiotics?<p>The side effects of antibiotics range from minor to very severe. Some of the common side effects include:</p><ul><li>Rash</li><li>Nausea</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Yeast <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span></li></ul><p>More serious side effects can include:</p><ul><li>C. diff <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>, which cause diarrhea that can lead to severe colon damage and sometimes even death</li><li>Severe and life-threatening allergic reactions</li><li>Antibiotic resistance <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span></li></ul><p>Call your health care provider if you develop any side effects while taking your antibiotic.</p>Why is it important to take antibiotics only when they're needed?<p>You should only take antibiotics when they are needed because they can cause side effects and can contribute to Antibiotic resistance <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>. Antibiotic resistance happens when the bacteria change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic. This means that the bacteria continue to grow.</p>How do I use antibiotics correctly?<p>When you take antibiotics, it is important that you take them responsibly:</p><ul><li>Always follow the directions carefully. Finish your medicine even if you feel better. If you stop taking them too soon, some bacteria may survive and re-infect you.</li><li>Don't save your antibiotics for later.</li><li>Don't share your antibiotic with others.</li><li>Don't take antibiotics prescribed for someone else. This may delay the best treatment for you, make you even sicker, or cause side effects.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/urinaryincontinence.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Urinary</span> Incontinence</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bladder Control</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Incontinence</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stress Incontinence</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bladder control problems</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">urinary</span> incontinence (UI)?<p><span class="qt0">Urinary</span> incontinence (UI) is the loss of bladder control, or being unable to control urination. It is a common condition. It can range from being a minor problem to something that greatly affects your daily life.  In any case, it can get better with proper treatment.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">urinary</span> incontinence (UI)?<p>There are several different types of UI. Each type has different symptoms and causes:</p><ul><li>Stress incontinence happens when stress or pressure on your bladder causes you to leak <span class="qt0">urine</span>.  This could be due to coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting something heavy, or physical activity. Causes include weak pelvic floor muscles and the bladder being out of its normal position.</li><li>Urge, or urgency, incontinence happens when you have a strong urge (need) to urinate, and some <span class="qt0">urine</span> leaks out before you can make it to the toilet. It is often related to an overactive bladder. Urge incontinence is most common in older people. It can sometimes be a sign of a <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> (UTI). It can also happen in some neurological conditions, such as multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injuries.</li><li>Overflow incontinence happens when your bladder doesn't empty all the way. This causes too much <span class="qt0">urine</span> to stay in your bladder. Your bladder gets too full, and you leak <span class="qt0">urine</span>. This form of UI is most common in men. Some of the causes include tumors, kidney stones, diabetes, and certain medicines.</li><li>Functional incontinence happens when a physical or mental disability, trouble speaking, or some other problem keeps you from getting to the toilet in time. For example, someone with arthritis may have trouble unbuttoning his or her pants, or a person with Alzheimer's disease may not realize they need to plan to use the toilet.</li><li>Mixed incontinence means that you have more than one type of incontinence. It's usually a combination of stress and urge incontinence.</li><li>Transient incontinence is <span class="qt0">urine</span> leakage that is caused by a temporary (transient) situation such as an <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> or new medicine. Once the cause is removed, the incontinence goes away.</li><li>Bedwetting refers to <span class="qt0">urine</span> leakage during sleep. This is most common in children, but adults can also have it.
   <ul><li>Bedwetting is normal for many children. It is more common in boys. Bedwetting is often not considered a health problem, especially when it runs in the family. But if it still happens often at age 5 and older, it may be because of a bladder control problem. This problem could be caused by slow physical development, an illness, making too much <span class="qt0">urine</span> at night, or another problem. Sometimes there is more than one cause.</li><li>In adults, the causes include some medicines, caffeine, and alcohol. It can also be caused by certain health problems, such as diabetes insipidus, a <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> (UTI), kidney stones, enlarged prostate (BPH), and sleep apnea.</li></ul>
</li></ul>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">urinary</span> incontinence (UI)?<p>In adults, you are at higher risk of developing UI if you:</p><ul><li>Are female, especially after going through pregnancy, childbirth, and/or menopause</li><li>Are older. As you age, your <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> muscles weaken, making it harder to hold in <span class="qt0">urine</span>.</li><li>Are a man with prostate problems</li><li>Have certain health problems, such as diabetes, obesity, or long-lasting constipation</li><li>Are a smoker</li><li>Have a birth defect that affects the structure of your <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span></li></ul><p>In children, bedwetting is more common in younger children, boys, and those whose parents wet the bed when they were children.</p>How is <span class="qt0">urinary</span> incontinence (UI) diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms. Your provider may ask you to keep a bladder diary for a few days before your appointment. The bladder diary includes how much and when you drink liquids, when and how much you urinate, and whether you leak <span class="qt0">urine</span>.</li><li>A physical exam, which can include a rectal exam. Women may also get a pelvic exam.</li><li><span class="qt0">Urine</span> and/or blood tests</li><li>Bladder function tests</li><li>Imaging tests</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">urinary</span> incontinence (UI)?<p>Treatment depends on the type and cause of your UI. You may need a combination of treatments. Your provider may first suggest self-care treatments, including:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes to reduce leaks:
        <ul><li>Drinking the right amount of liquid at the right time</li><li>Being physically active</li><li>Staying at a healthy weigh</li><li>Avoiding constipation</li><li>Not smoking</li></ul>
</li><li>Bladder training. This involves urinating according to a schedule. Your provider makes a schedule from you, based on information from your bladder diary. After you adjust to the schedule, you gradually wait a little longer between trips to the bathroom. This can help stretch your bladder so it can hold more <span class="qt0">urine</span>.</li><li>Doing exercises to strengthen your pelvic floor muscles. Strong pelvic floor muscles hold in <span class="qt0">urine</span> better than weak muscles. The strengthening exercises are called Kegel exercises. They involve tightening and relaxing the muscles that control <span class="qt0">urine</span> flow.</li></ul><p>If these treatments do not work, your provider may suggest other options such as:</p><ul><li>Medicines, which can be used to
        <ul><li>Relax the bladder muscles, to help prevent bladder spasms</li><li>Block nerve signals that cause <span class="qt0">urinary</span> frequency and urgency</li><li>In men, shrink the prostate and improve <span class="qt0">urine</span> flow</li></ul></li><li>Medical devices, including
        <ul><li>A catheter, which is a tube to carry <span class="qt0">urine</span> out of the body. You might use one a few times a day or all the time.</li><li>For women, a ring or a tampon-like device inserted into the vagina. The devices pushes up against your urethra to help decrease leaks.</li></ul></li><li>Bulking agents, which are injected into the bladder neck and urethra tissues to thicken them. This helps close your bladder opening so you have less leaking.</li><li>Electrical nerve stimulation, which involves changing your bladder's reflexes using pulses of electricity</li><li>Surgery to support the bladder in its normal position. This may be done with a sling that is attached to the pubic bone.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/prostatediseases.html">
      <content name="title">Prostate Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is the prostate?<p>The prostate is a gland in the male reproductive system. It lies just below the bladder. It makes fluid that is part of semen.</p>What are prostate diseases?<p>There are many types of prostate diseases:</p><p>
</p><ul><li>Prostatitis is inflammation (swelling and pain) in the prostate gland. It's the most common type of prostate problem in people under than age 50. There are different types: 
	<ul><li>Chronic prostatitis is also called chronic pelvic pain syndrome. It's the most common type of prostatitis.</li><li>Acute bacterial prostatitis starts suddenly from a bacterial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> and is treated with antibiotics. It is not common.</li><li>Chronic bacterial prostatitis happens when a bacterial <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> keeps coming back. The symptoms usually start slowly. It may take longer to treat than acute bacterial prostatitis.</li><li>Asymptomatic prostatitis has no symptoms and usually doesn't need treatment. You may learn you have it after having tests for other health problems.</li></ul>
</li><li>Enlarged prostate is also called benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). The prostate gland tends to grow larger with age. That's why enlarged prostate is very common in older people and rare in those who are under age 40. When the prostate grows larger, it may press on your urethra and cause problems with urination.</li><li>Prostate cancer happens when cancer cells form in the prostate gland. Prostate cancer is a common type of cancer in those aged 50 and older. Most prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause health problems. But certain prostate cancers are serious.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop prostate diseases?<p>Anyone with a prostate can develop prostate problems. But some people are at higher risk.</p><p>You may be more likely to develop prostatitis if you have:</p><ul><li>A lower <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span>, also called a UTI. An <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span> in your lower <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> (bladder and urethra) may lead to acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis.</li><li>Nerve damage in your lower <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> from surgery or an injury. This may lead to chronic prostatitis.</li><li>Emotional stress, which can lead to chronic prostatitis.</li></ul><p>You may be more likely to develop an enlarged prostate (BPH) if you:</p><ul><li>Are age 40 or older.</li><li>Have family members who have had BPH.</li><li>Have certain health conditions such as:
	<ul><li>Obesity.</li><li>Heart disease and problems with blood circulation.</li><li>Type 2 diabetes.</li></ul>
</li><li>Don't get enough physical activity.</li></ul><p>You may be more likely to develop prostate cancer if you:</p><ul><li>Are older than age 50.</li><li>Have a parent, sibling, or child who has or had prostate cancer.</li><li>Are African American.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of prostate diseases?<p>The symptoms of prostate problems include:</p><ul><li>Needing to urinate a lot.</li><li>Needing to rush to the bathroom, but not being able to urinate or only going a little.</li><li>Leaking or dribbling <span class="qt0">urine</span>.</li><li>Having a weak <span class="qt0">urine</span> stream.</li></ul><p>Other symptoms depend on the type of prostate problem you have and may include:</p><ul><li>Not being able to urinate at all. This is a medical emergency.</li><li>Any problems, starting or controlling <span class="qt0">urine</span> flow.</li><li>Waking up often to urinate.</li><li>Blood in your <span class="qt0">urine or urine</span> that has an unusual smell or color.</li><li>Fever, chills, or body aches.</li><li>Great discomfort or pain:
	<ul><li>While urinating or after ejaculation.</li><li>In your abdomen (belly), between your scrotum and anus, or in your scrotum or penis.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Contact your provider if you have any of these symptoms.</p>How are prostate diseases diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have a prostate problem, your provider will:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history and symptoms.</li><li>Ask about your family health history.</li><li>Do a physical exam. The exam may include a digital rectal exam (DRE) of your prostate. In a DRE, your provider inserts a gloved finger into your rectum to feel the general size and condition of your prostate.</li><li>Order tests, if needed. Tests may include:
	<ul><li>Blood and <span class="qt0">urine</span> tests to look for <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span>.</li><li>Urodynamic testing to see how well you can hold and release <span class="qt0">urine</span>.</li><li>Cystoscopy to look inside your urethra and bladder.</li><li>Ultrasound pictures of your prostate and <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span>.</li><li>A PSA blood test (prostate-specific antigen test).</li><li>Prostate biopsy to diagnose or rule out cancer.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Treatment depends on what prostate disease you have and which symptoms bother you most.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/delirium.html">
      <content name="title">Delirium</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is delirium?<p>Delirium is a mental state in which you are confused, disoriented, and not able to think or remember clearly. It usually starts suddenly. It is often temporary and treatable.</p><p>There are three types of delirium:</p><ul><li>Hypoactive, when you are not active and seem sleepy, tired, or depressed</li><li>Hyperactive, when you are restless or agitated</li><li>Mixed, when you change back and forth between being hypoactive and hyperactive</li></ul>What causes delirium?<p>There are many different problems that can cause delirium. Some of the more common causes include:</p><ul><li>Advanced cancer.</li><li>Alcohol or drugs, either from intoxication or withdrawal. This includes a serious type of alcohol withdrawal syndrome called delirium tremens. It usually happens to people who stop drinking after years of alcohol use disorder (AUD).</li><li>Dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.</li><li>Dementia.</li><li>Hospitalization, especially in intensive care.</li><li><span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">Infections</span></span>, such as <span class="qt0">urinary</span> <span class="qt1">tract</span> <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infections</span></span>, pneumonia, and the flu.</li><li>Medicines. This could be a side effect of a medicine, such as sedatives or opioids. Or it could be from withdrawal after stopping a medicine.</li><li>Metabolic disorders.</li><li>Organ failure, such as kidney or liver failure.</li><li>Poisoning.</li><li>Serious illnesses.</li><li>Severe pain.</li><li>Sleep deprivation.</li><li>Surgeries, including reactions to anesthesia.</li></ul>Who is more likely to get delirium?<p>Certain factors put you at risk for delirium, including:</p><ul><li>Being in a hospital or nursing home</li><li>Having dementia</li><li>Having a serious illness or more than one illness</li><li>Having an <span class="qt2"><span class="qt3">infection</span></span></li><li>Older age</li><li>Having surgery</li><li>Taking medicines that affect the mind or behavior</li><li>Taking high doses of pain medicines, such as opioids</li></ul>What are the symptoms of delirium?<p>The symptoms of delirium usually start suddenly, over a few hours or a few days. They often come and go. The most common symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Changes in alertness (usually more alert in the morning, less at night)</li><li>Changing levels of consciousness</li><li>Confusion</li><li>Disorganized thinking, talking in a way that doesn't make sense</li><li>Disrupted sleep patterns, sleepiness</li><li>Emotional changes: anger, agitation, depression, irritability, overexcitement</li><li>Hallucinations and delusions</li><li>Memory problems, especially with short-term memory</li><li>Trouble concentrating</li></ul>How is delirium diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>Physical and neurological exams</li><li>Mental status testing, which checks for problems with your thinking and alertness </li><li>Lab and  diagnostic imaging tests</li></ul><p>Delirium and dementia have similar symptoms, so it can be hard to tell them apart. You can also have both at the same time. The differences between them are that:</p><ul><li>Delirium starts suddenly and can cause hallucinations. It is mainly a problem with attention and staying alert. The symptoms may get better or worse and can last for hours or weeks.</li><li>Dementia develops slowly and does not cause hallucinations. It usually starts with memory loss. The symptoms don't change often, like they can with delirium. Dementia almost never gets better.</li></ul>What are the treatments for delirium?<p>Treatment of delirium focuses on the causes and symptoms of delirium. The first step is to identify the cause. Often, treating the cause will lead to a full recovery. The recovery may take some time - weeks or sometimes even months. In the meantime, there may be treatments to manage the symptoms, such as:</p><ul><li>Controlling the environment, which includes making sure that the room is quiet and well-lit, having clocks or calendars in view, and having family members around</li><li>Medicines, including those that control aggression or agitation and pain relievers if there is pain</li><li>If needed, making sure that the person has a hearing aid, glasses, or other devices for communication</li></ul>Can delirium be prevented?<p>Treating the conditions that can cause delirium may reduce the risk of getting it. Hospitals can help lower the risk of delirium by avoiding sedatives and making sure that hospital rooms are kept quiet, calm, and well-lit. It can also help to have family members around and to have the same staff members treat the person each day (if possible).</p></content>
